description: The objective of the Rodent Research-5 (RR-5) study was to evaluate bone loss in mice during spaceflight and to determine if treatment with a modified version of NEL-like molecule-1 (NELL-1) can reduce or prevent bone loss that would otherwise occur during spaceflight. To this end, a cohort of forty 30-weeks-old female BALB/cAnNTac mice were flown to the ISS and housed in the Rodent Habitat. Six days after launch half of the mice were treated with NELL-1 (10 mg/kg in 0.3 ml PBS), while the other half were treated with vehicle control (0.3 mls PBS). Fourteen days after launch animals were again treated with NELL-1 or vehicle control as before, except that all animals were also injected with the bone marker, calcein green (20 mg/kg in 0.1 ml). Injections of vehicle, NELL-1, and bone markers were intraperitoneal. After all forty mice on orbit received two treatments; ten control mice and ten experimental mice were randomly selected for live animal return (LAR). At approximately 30 days after launch the twenty LAR mice were transported live back to Earth. Animals were allowed to recover for 30 days in standard habitats before euthanasia via intraperitoneal injection with ketamine/xylazine. During the recovery, the animals received another two treatments. GeneLab received RNA later preserved dorsal skin from ten live animal return and ten matching ground control mice. These were from the vehicle control animals only. RNA was extracted, libraries generated (stranded, ribodepleted) and sequenced (target 60 M clusters at PE 150 bp).
funding: The sequencing analysis was funded by NASA Space Biology Program Office, Space Life and Physical Sciences Research and Applications Division.

payloads.description:
RR-5 launched 40 mice (~32 weeks old, female, BALB/c) on SpX11 to determine if treatment with NELL1 can reduce or prevent bone loss. 20 mice were maintained for ~30 days in microgravity and then returned live (Live Animal Return-LAR) for dissection at the PI institution and the other 20 mice were maintained in microgravity for ~9 weeks and dissected on-orbit. Samples from the Systemic Therapy of NELL-1 for osteoporosis returned as part of an investigation using rodents as models to test a new drug that can both rebuild bone and block further bone loss, improving crew health. When people and animals spend extended periods of time in space, they experience bone density loss, or osteoporosis. In-flight countermeasures, such as exercise, prevent it from getting worse, but there isn't a therapy on Earth or in space that can restore bone density. The results from this ISS National Laboratory-sponsored investigation are built on previous research also supported by the National Institutes for Health and could lead to new drugs for treating bone density loss in millions of people on Earth.

The mission objectives

The objective of the Rodent Research-5 (RR-5) study was to evaluate bone loss in mice under microgravity conditions and to determine if treatment with NELL1 can reduce or prevent bone loss that would otherwise occur in microgravity. RR-5 launched 40 mice (~32 weeks old, female, BALB/c) on SpX11 to determine if treatment with NELL1 can reduce or prevent bone loss. 20 mice were maintained for ~30 days in microgravity and then returned live (Live Animal Return-LAR) for dissection at the PI institution and the other 20 mice were maintained in microgravity for ~9 weeks and dissected on-orbit. 

All animal procedures performed in these experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees (IACUC) number NAS-16-001-Y1 for flight at the NASA Ames Research Center (ARC) and the Kennedy Space Center (KSC) and the methods were carried out in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations.

The Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS) has formed a partnership with the University of California at Los Angeles (UCLA) to evaluate bone atrophy under microgravity conditions and to evaluate a novel therapeutic to mitigate bone loss. Samples from the Systemic Therapy of NELL-1 for osteoporosis returned as part of an investigation using rodents as models to test a new drug that can both rebuild bone and block further bone loss, improving crew health. When people and animals spend extended periods of time in space, they experience bone density loss, or osteoporosis. In-flight countermeasures, such as exercise, prevent it from getting worse, but there isn't a therapy on Earth or in space that can restore bone density. The results from this ISS National Laboratory-sponsored investigation are built on previous research also supported by the National Institutes for Health and could lead to new drugs for treating bone density loss in millions of people on Earth.

IACUC Protocol Number:  NAS-16-001-Y1

All animal procedures performed in these experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and use Committees (IACUC) numbers NASA: NAS-16-001-Y1 for flight at the NASA Ames Research Center (ARC) and the Kennedy Space Center (KSC) and the methods were carried out in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations.

NASA Space Biology Biospecimen Sharing Program Activities 
The NASA Space Biology Biospecimen Sharing Program collected biospecimens from RR-5 to maximize the scientific return from the biological spaceflight. Forty mice (female; BALB/c; 32 weeks old; Taconic), launched in two Transporters (20 mice per), then were transferred to Rodent Habitats onboard the International Space Station (ISS) and maintained in microgravity for ~30 days until Live Animal Return (N-20; LAR to UCLA) or for ~9 weeks total which were ISS Terminal (N-20; IT). There was a Baseline of subjects at KSC. A Ground Control group mimicked LAR, which was housed at KSC, then shipped live to UCLA. There was a Ground Control group at KSC which mimicked flight. All animals were kept on a temperature controlled (~28˚C), 12-hr Light/Dark Cycle.

The unused Diaphragm and tail tissues were set to the NASA Biological Institutional Scientific Collection and made available for request.


Available Data

The RR-5 payload produced the following Data (from checklist Excel file):

-	Animal enclosure temperature and relative humidity flight and ground data
-	Live Animal Return sensor accelerometer data 
-	ISS cabin and ground simulation chamber environmental monitoring data  
-	Rodent data including preflight data, operations time logs, sample shipment data.
-	Flight and ground animal behavior video, available for request.

protocols.description: A cohort of 30 weeks-old female BALB/c mice (Taconic) were flown to the ISS on June 3rd, 2017 and were housed in the Rodent Habitat for around 30 days before returned to earth alive. All the animals from which the samples were sequenced in this dataset received two sham treatment in ISS: on Launch+6 days (L+6 days), vehicle control treatment (0.3mL of PBS) was administered intraperitoneally. The second treatment was administered two weeks after launch with vehicle control injection (0.3mL of PBS) followed by 0.1 mL of Calcein (bone marker).  Upon live animal return, mice were transported to the PI's UCLA lab on July 4th, 2017.  Upon arrival, a behaviroal test was performed and Dual-energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DXA) scan was performed while the animals were anesthestized by ketamine/xylazine. Upon completion of the scan, the mice received an injection of 0.2mL Atipamezole to allow recovery. The third treatment was administered with vehicle treatment (0.3mL of PBS) followed by 0.1 mL of Alizarin Red (bone marker). At around six weeks after launch, the fourth treatment was administered with vehicle control injection (0.3mL of PBS) followed by 0.1 mL of Calcein (bone marker). The animals were housed in the vivarium cages for around 30 days until experiment termination. The last DXA scan was performed right before termination.  Ground controls were conducted on a 3-day delay at Kennedy Space Center in ISS Environmental Simulators (ISSES) programmed with data from the Dragon capsule and the ISS cabin. The ground control animals received the same treatments as flight animals. After ~30 days housing in the Rodent Habitat, the ground control animals were shipped from KSC to PI's UCLA lab and were housed for 30 days in the vivarium cages until experiment termination.
protocols.name: animal husbandry

protocols.description: Mice were euthanized by intraperitoneal injection of ketamine/xylazine. Dissection was performed at UCLA.  Skin tissues used for extraction were preserved in RNAlater after dissection and stored at -80C. The frozen preserved skin tissues were shipped frozen to NASA Ames Research Center and handled by BSP and LSDA.
protocols.name: sample collection

protocols.description: RNA was extracted using the modified Trizol protocol from Dr. Masahiro Terada. Frozen skin, approximately 60 mg weight, were cut into small pieces. Transfered cut pieces into tube containing 1.6 mL cold Trizol. Samples were homogenized for 20 seconds at 21,000 rpm using a Polytron PT1300D (Kinematica, Bohemia, NY) handheld homogenizer with 5 mm standard dispersing aggregate tip. Homogenates were centrifuged at 15,000 g for 10 minutes at 4C to remove cell debris. Supernatant from each sample was split into 2 technical replicates and used to isolate RNA. Chloroform was added for phase separation and RNA was captured using isopropyl alcohol and Ethachinmate(Fujifilm Wako Chemicals). RNA was washed twice with 75% ethanol and eluted in 20 uL of RNase-free water. Eluted technical replicates were combined. Concentration of RNA was measured using the Qubit 3 Fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with Qubit RNA BR kit. RNA quality was assessed using the Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer with the Agilent RNA 6000 Nano Kit (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA).
protocols.name: nucleic acid extraction

protocols.description: ERCC ExFold RNA Spike-In Mixes (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA Cat # 4456739, v92) at 1:100 dilution of either Mix 1 or Mix 2 were added immediately after RNA extractions at the concentrations suggested by the manufacturer protocol.
protocols.name: spike-in protocol

protocols.description: RNA ribo depletion was done with Illumina TruSeq Stranded Total RNA Library Prep Gold. Input RNA were approximately 500 ng with RIN greater than 4. Index adapters were 1.5 uM (IDT, 384-well xGen Dual Index UMI Adapters). 15 cycles PCR were performed. Library fragment size ~300 bp was assessed using Agilent 4200 TapeStation with D1000 DNA ScreenTape (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA). Pooled library concentration was measured by Universal qPCR Master Mix (Kapa Biosystems, Wilmington, MA). Library quality control was determined by iSeq100 (Illumina, San Diego, CA).
protocols.name: library construction

protocols.description: RNA sequencing was performed by GeneLab Sample Processing Lab on Illumina NovaSeq 6000. Paired end 149bp. PhiX included as control.
protocols.name: nucleic acid sequencing

protocols.description: Quality assessment of reads was performed with FastQC v0.12.1 and reports were combined with MultiQC v1.26. rRNA percentages of reads were estimated with the 'hts_SeqScreener' program of htstream v1.0.0.
protocols.name: GeneLab raw data processing protocol

protocols.description: Data were processed as described in GL-DPPD-7101-G (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/master/RNAseq/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7101_Versions/GL-DPPD-7101-G.md), using NF_RCP version 2.1.0 (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_RNASeq_Workflow/tree/NF_RCP_2.1.0). In short, raw fastq files were filtered using Trim Galore! (version 0.6.10) powered by Cutadapt (version 4.2). Trimmed fastq file quality was evaluated with FastQC (version 0.12.1), and MultiQC (version 1.26) was used to generate MultiQC reports. Mus Musculus STAR and RSEM references were built using STAR (version 2.7.11b) and RSEM (version 1.3.3), respectively, Ensembl release 112, genome assembly GRCm39 (Mus_musculus.GRCm39.dna.primary_assembly.fa) concatenated with ERCC92.fa from ThermoFisher (https://assets.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/LSG/manuals/ERCC92.zip), and the following gtf annotation file: Mus_musculus.GRCm39.112.gtf concatenated with the ERCC92.gtf file from ThermoFisher (https://assets.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/LSG/manuals/ERCC92.zip). Trimmed reads were aligned to the Mus Musculus + ERCC STAR reference with STAR (version 2.7.11b) and alignment log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). Aligned reads were assessed for strandedness using RSeQC infer_experiment.py (version 5.0.4), gene body coverage using RSeQC geneBody_coverage.py (version 5.0.4), inner distance was assessed using RSeQC inner_distance.py (version 5.0.4), and distribution of RNA features using RSeQC read_distribution.py (version 5.0.4). Aligned reads from all samples were quantified using RSEM (version 1.3.3), with strandedness set to forward and RSEM count log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). To create a set of rRNA-removed quantification data, Ensembl IDs mapping to ribosomal RNA (rRNA) were removed from the RSEM gene count data. Both the original set of RSEM quantification data and the rRNA-removed data were subject to differential gene expression analysis as follows. A runsheet was generated with dp_tools (version 1.3.8) and the runsheet and quantification data were imported to R (version 4.4.2) with tximport (version 1.34.0), ERCC genes were removed, and the non-ERCC genes were normalized with DESeq2 (version 1.46.0) median of ratios method. Normalized gene counts were subject to differential expression analysis. Differential expression analysis was performed in R (version 4.4.2) using DESeq2 (version 1.46.0); all groups were compared pairwise using the Wald test and the likelihood ratio test was used to generate the F statistic p-value. Gene annotations were assigned using the custom annotation tables generated in-house as detailed in GL-DPPD-7110-A (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/GL_RefAnnotTable-A_1.1.0/GeneLab_Reference_Annotations/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7110_Versions/GL-DPPD-7110-A/GL-DPPD-7110-A.md), with STRINGdb (version 2.16.4), PANTHER.db (version 1.0.12), and org.Mm.eg.db (version 3.19.1). Assessment of ERCC spiked genes was performed as detailed in the ERCC_analysis_GLbulkRNAseq.html report.
